title: Mirabel and the Cipher
premise: Ada Kavanagh, archivist of St. Verena's Cathedral, catalogues the dead for a living — until a confession letter arrives postmarked the day after a stranger's funeral, claiming the man was murdered and naming Ada as the only person who can prove it. Following the letter's clues, Ada discovers the cathedral's locked crypt conceals a ledger written in cipher: decades of forged deaths, identities erased and sold to people desperate to vanish. As Ada decodes it, he realizes his own late brother's name appears in its pages — and that someone is killing everyone who ever bought an ending. The killer is the crypt's former keeper, now the cathedral's beloved canon, who has been 'collecting' the escaped lives to protect the secret; in the climax Ada traps him inside the crypt he sealed, choosing truth over the mercy of forgetting.
about_author: Wren Lockridge is a former parish records clerk who spent eleven years transcribing burial registers before turning to fiction. They write mysteries about paper trails, quiet buildings, and the things people bury on purpose.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Ada Kavanagh's POV. While cataloguing funeral ephemera at St. Verena's, Ada receives a confession letter postmarked the day after Thomas Ellery's funeral — from Ellery himself, claiming he was murdered and that the proof sleeps beneath the locked crypt. The emotional beat is cold disbelief curdling into compulsion: Ada, who trusts paper over people, cannot put this letter down.

chapters.title: The Locked Crypt
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada petitions Canon Merrick Hale for access to the crypt, sealed since a 1970s structural collapse, and is gently but firmly refused. Exploring the archive instead, Ada finds Ellery's burial record contains an impossible detail: his death date matches a ledger entry forty years old. The beat is unease — the first crack in the official story.

chapters.title: A Stranger's Funeral
chapters.summary: Ada attends Ellery's funeral under a pretext, observing the mourners: a weeping woman who seems to be performing grief, and a man who watches Ada watching her. POV shifts briefly to the woman, Ruth Ellery, who knows the body in the casket isn't her husband. The beat is disorientation — everyone here is lying about something.

chapters.title: Ledger in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Re-reading the confession, Ada follows its hint to the cathedral's donor plaques and memorial brasses, realizing their dates and initials form a substitution cipher. Decoded fragments reference 'the Ledger' and 'the Keeper.' The beat is intellectual thrill shadowed by dread: the building itself has been keeping secrets.

chapters.title: What Ada Buried
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter in Ada's POV, revealing his brother Daniel's disappearance twenty years ago and Ada's guilt over the unanswered questions. He came to St. Verena's partly because Daniel once wrote him from this city. The beat is grief made functional — Ada admits the case has become personal, which makes him dangerous to himself.

chapters.title: The Widow Who Wasn't
chapters.summary: Ruth Ellery's POV. Ruth confronts Ada privately: the man buried as her husband was a stranger she'd been paid to marry, part of an arrangement she never fully understood. She gives Ada Ellery's last appointment book. The beat is wary alliance between two people who both profited from a lie they didn't write.

chapters.title: Forty Years of Endings
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Cross-referencing the appointment book with the plaque-cipher, Ada reconstructs the Ledger's purpose: a service selling legal deaths to people who needed to vanish, run from the crypt by its keeper. Dozens of names, dozens of new identities. The beat is vertigo — the scale of the secret dwarfs one murder.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Hand
chapters.summary: Ada notices the cipher's handwriting matches archival documents signed by a young Merrick Hale — the canon himself. But when Ada probes Hale obliquely, the old man seems genuinely baffled, even frightened. The beat is doubt: either Hale is a brilliant liar, or someone else held the pen.

chapters.title: Second Death
chapters.summary: Detective Inspector Soraya Nkemelu's POV. A second death: Martin Oduya, found drowned, another name from Ada's decoded list. Nkemelu interviews Ada and notes his obsession with the crypt. The beat is rising stakes — the list is being worked through, and Ada's research may be painting targets.

chapters.title: Bought Names
chapters.summary: Ada tracks a surviving name from the Ledger: Vivian Marsh, living quietly two towns over under a purchased identity. Marsh confirms the service was real, describes the masked 'Keeper' who administered it, and warns Ada to stop. The beat is survivor's terror — the price of survival is silence, and silence is failing.

chapters.title: Daniel's Page
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Decoding deeper into the Ledger, Ada finds his brother Daniel's name — recorded not as a client but as an apprentice to the Keeper, dated weeks before his disappearance. The beat is devastation reframed as hope: Daniel didn't vanish; he was recruited, and may have lived years Ada never knew about.

chapters.title: The Confession's Second Half
chapters.summary: Ada discovers the letter he received was only half of Ellery's confession; the other half was mailed to someone else. Tracing the second envelope, he learns it went to Canon Hale — meaning Ellery tried to blackmail the church itself. The beat is dread tightening: Ellery died of what he knew, not just what he did.

chapters.title: Nkemelu's File
chapters.summary: DI Nkemelu's POV. Nkemelu pulls the 1970s 'structural collapse' file and finds the engineer's report was falsified — the crypt was sealed to hide something, not to protect anyone. She begins quietly connecting Ada's archive requests to two murders. The beat is institutional rot surfacing, and a detective deciding to trust an amateur.

chapters.title: Night in the Nave
chapters.summary: Ada breaks into the cathedral after hours to photograph the full plaque sequence, and is nearly caught by someone moving in the dark — he escapes with partial photographs and a torn scrap of modern paper bearing fresh cipher. The beat is fear sharpening into certainty: the Keeper is still active, still writing.

chapters.title: The Living Client
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The torn scrap decodes to a current client intake record — someone bought a death within the last year. Ada identifies them as a prominent local philanthropist about to be honored by the cathedral. The beat is moral complexity: the victim of exposure may be innocent of everything except wanting out.

chapters.title: Hale Breaks
chapters.summary: Confronted with the falsified report, Canon Hale confesses partially: as a young priest he discovered the Ledger and chose to protect the church's reputation rather than its souls, sealing the crypt and burning nothing. He swears he isn't the present-day Keeper. The beat is tragic complicity — good men maintaining bad architecture.

chapters.title: The Apprentice's Trail
chapters.summary: Ada follows Daniel's apprentice records to a storage unit rented under a cipher-name for twenty years: inside are the true Ledger, correspondence, and unsent letters from Daniel to Ada, proving Daniel discovered the Keeper was murdering clients who tried to leave the service — and that Daniel planned to expose him. The beat is heartbreak and fury fused.

chapters.title: Who Kept the Keys
chapters.summary: Ada realizes the only person with continuous crypt access across four decades is the cathedral's mild sexton, Edmund Voss — Daniel's old supervisor, the man who reported him missing. Voss has been 'retiring' clients ever since. The beat is horror wearing a familiar face: the killer has been emptying Ada's wastebaskets for months.

chapters.title: The Philanthropist's Hour
chapters.summary: Voss moves against the newest client during the cathedral's honors ceremony, planning a staged accident. Ada and Nkemelu race to intervene; they save the client but Voss slips away into the cathedral's lower levels, taking the Ledger's final pages. The beat is public chaos masking private pursuit.

chapters.title: Into the Crypt
chapters.summary: Ada descends alone into the unlocked crypt, following Voss, and finds Daniel's final hiding place — evidence Daniel died there twenty years ago protecting the Ledger. Voss corners Ada among the coffins, offering the same bargain once offered to Daniel: forget, and live. The beat is the theme made flesh at knifepoint.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Climax. Ada refuses the bargain, stalls Voss with the truth aloud — recorded by Nkemelu, who followed — and triggers the crypt's failing mechanism, trapping Voss until police arrive. In the struggle Ada nearly chooses vengeance over testimony, and chooses otherwise. The beat is the cost paid in full: survival without erasure.

chapters.title: Every Name Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Resolution. Weeks later, the Ledger becomes evidence and then memorial: Ada reads every purchased name aloud at a service of restoration, including Daniel's, finally grieved properly. Ruth Ellery reclaims her own name; Hale resigns; Ada remains archivist, keeper now of truths instead of locks. The beat is quiet, earned peace — memory kept, identity returned, survival no longer a debt.
